New here? What every word on this page means — start with Promising?.

Click a column heading to sort; type in the row beneath it to filter. Numeric columns take a comparison (>100, <=-20); a bare number means >=. Everything else matches on substring. Rows with no recorded run sort last and fail every numeric filter.

Promising? is our own checklist, run automatically — not an opinion, and not "whichever number is biggest". Not a candidate: a measuring tool, never traded. Unproven: never tested against random luck, or a luck test was run and could not give an answer — neither is a failure. Not promising: it loses money, or it fails the luck test, or it is worse than our best strategy on both reward-for-risk and worst drop — a bigger gain bought with a bigger hole is not an improvement. Promising: makes money, beats luck, and is not worse on both. Even that only earns a trial run — every figure here comes from replaying past prices, and none of it has been traded.
Every figure here assumes you buy at the next morning's open. That choice is not a detail. Buying the same signals with an order left slightly below last night's close instead — which is how you would really trade this — costs our best strategy two thirds of its gain (+133.4% → +46.9%) and makes its worst drop deeper. Only about 59% of those orders ever fill, and the ones that miss are the days the price jumped and ran. The strategies that improve under it are the ones with no edge to lose — and not one of them stops losing money.

TV and Stockbit count how many of a strategy's buying conditions each screener can actually set up, out of the total. Sorting the results is left out — no screener does that step. A screen built from only some of the rules gives you a longer list than the strategy, never a shorter one, so it is a watchlist builder and not the strategy itself. READ THE TWO COLUMNS AS EITHER, NOT BOTH. The house rule is that one screener has to express the whole rule — whichever one. A strategy reading 3 / 5 on TV and 5 / 5 on Stockbit is fully runnable, on Stockbit; the low number is not a shortfall and does not make it 60% of a strategy. What it does decide is WHERE the screen is run, and running it on the other one would be a different rule.

3.2 ★ bs_tv_sb_trend_tv_ma20

1d · nulls S✓ T✓ · fwd not_run

Verdict · PROVED END TO END on the owner's instruction, and the honest summary is that it CLEARS EVERY BAR AND EARNS ALMOST NOTHING. It beats the standing benchmark on both primary axes, but barely, and it is the only one of the three current challengers whose BOTH luck tests could be run and were passed -- so it has the strongest evidence and the smallest effect. WHAT IT IS: the benchmark plus one extra condition, that price is also above its twenty-day average. Everything else is byte-identical to the benchmark. THE CATCH, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT: this arm was NOT declared before it was run. It is the survivor of a ten-way search over filters, nine of which lost. Picking the winner of a search and presenting it as a hypothesis is how a repo talks itself into noise, and the measurement agrees: once the deflated-Sharpe calculation accounts for how many things have been tried here, its score and the benchmark's are both a whisker above zero and effectively tied. Regenerate that with the deflated Sharpe tool; never copy the figure, it moves with every arm anyone adds. IT DOES NOT FIX THE BENCHMARK'S WORST PROPERTY. It still loses money in the middle of the three periods the history is split into, and still reads REGIME-DEPENDENT. IT ALSO LEAVES THE BIG IMPROVEMENT ON THE TABLE. Nudging its own thresholds shows the same one-way slope on the volume condition that the other two strategies had -- looser is better, all the way to the edge of the test. Adding a moving-average condition did not remove that; deleting the volume condition did, and that is what the two rankvol strategies are. WHAT IT IS NOT: a higher-probability setup. Win rate is unchanged against the benchmark. The gain is in expectancy, and it comes from reallocating position slots rather than from avoiding losers. Replayed past prices, never traded, no unseen data. Whether it is adopted is the owner's decision.

3.3 ★ bs_tv_sb_trend_tv_ma20_ext10

1d · nulls S✓ T✓ · fwd not_run

Verdict · NOT A CANDIDATE -- failed its own pre-registered test (the extension-cap pass, docs/BENCHMARK_CHALLENGERS.md). The added rule -- never buy far above the stock's recent average price -- made this strategy clearly worse on both reward-for-risk and its worst losing stretch, because it throws away about half the stocks the strategy normally picks from. It beat the luck tests; that does not rescue it, because the test it failed was the comparison against its own parent, not against luck. Kept as recorded evidence.

dist_sma_20 <= 10 [unverified]

Rule: Price <= 1.1 x Price MA 20

dist_sma_20 <= X is close/sma_20 <= 1 + X/100, i.e. "Price <= (1 + X/100) x Price MA 20". The threshold the recipe shows is already converted from idxbt's signed percentage (e.g. 10) to Stockbit's multiplier (1.1) -- typing idxbt's raw 10 into Stockbit would pass almost the whole market. NOT an exact equivalence, and this was measured rather than assumed: `python3 -c "import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_parquet('data/panel/ features_1d.parquet', columns=['close','sma_20','dist_sma_20']); a = df['dist_sma_20'] <= 10; b = df['close'] <= 1.10 * df['sma_20']; known = df['sma_20'].notna(); print((a[known] != b[known]).sum(), known.sum())"` currently prints `37 1257791` against the 2026-08-28 daily panel -- every disagreement sits at the exact tie close/sma_20 == 1.10, which is float64 rounding on a boundary, not a design gap. The other 302209 rows are NaN warm-up (no 20-bar SMA yet); `NaN <= 10` is False on both sides, so warm-up is excluded rather than admitted by either form. Re-run the command above against whichever panel is current rather than trusting this count. WHY verified IS false, and it is NOT because the mapping is doubted. Every PART of this rule is verified -- `Price` and `Price MA 20` are both verified Stockbit filters, and the `[field] [op] [multiplier] x [field]` shape is exercised by the verified `vol_ratio_50` mapping (`Volume >= 1.5 x Volume MA 50`). The COMPOSITION is not; nobody has opened Stockbit and typed `Price <= 1.1 x Price MA 20`. That is a deduction, and this file's own history is a list of deductions about screener fields that turned out wrong -- the retracted "atr" absence, and the Stoch RSI that exists and answers a different question. The term stays expressible and UNVERIFIED, which is what `Recipe.unverified` reports. ONE logged-in check flips it to true. Downgraded from verified:true on review, 2026-09-02.

Then rank by vol_ratio_50 — highest first, keep 10. No screener does this step, and it is not counted above.

3.6 ★ trend_ma2_rankvol

1d · nulls S✓ T✓ · fwd not_run

Verdict · WHAT IT IS, IN ONE LINE: our best strategy with one rule deleted, and nothing else changed. The deleted rule said 'only buy if today's trading volume is well above this stock's normal volume'. WHY DELETING IT HELPED: the strategy already SORTS its candidates by volume and keeps the top ten. So that rule's only remaining job was to leave a slot empty when not enough names had a volume spike. The names it was turning away did better than the empty slot. Put simply, waiting for the volume spike means buying after the move has already started. WHAT CHANGED: it makes more money AND its worst losing stretch is smaller. That combination is unusual -- normally a bigger gain costs you bigger swings. It also made money in all three periods we split the history into, where the strategy it came from lost money in one of them. It buys about as often, costs about the same in fees, and needs about the same number of days at the screen. HOW SURE ARE WE: it now passes BOTH luck tests, which is the strongest statement this project makes about a strategy. Random stock picking on its own buying days loses heavily, and so does buying random names on random days -- it beat every single one of the fake runs on both. Its earlier 'could not answer' on the timing test was a fault in that test, since fixed, and not a mark against this strategy. Nudging its remaining numbers up and down by a fifth barely moves the result, so it is not balanced on a knife edge. WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN: this is a replay of prices that had already happened when the rule was written. It has never been traded and has not been tried on a single day of unseen data. On our own rules that earns it a trial run and nothing more. Whether it gets one is the owner's decision.

3.8 ★ trend_ma3_rankvol

1d · nulls S✓ T✓ · fwd not_run

Verdict · NO EFFECT, and that is the pre-registered verdict, not a disappointment. This is the combination of the two changes that each helped on their own: add 'price also above its twenty-day average', and delete 'only buy on above-normal volume'. WHAT WAS DECLARED BEFORE IT RAN: the twenty-day condition would count as earning its place only if it improved reward-for-risk by a clear margin over the simpler strategy that already has the volume gate removed. It improved it by well under that margin. So by the rule written in advance, THE SIMPLER RULE STANDS and this one is recorded rather than adopted. WHAT THE RULE WRITTEN IN ADVANCE COULD NOT SEE, AND THIS IS THE HONEST PART: its worst losing stretch is by far the smallest of any strategy here -- roughly a third shallower than the simpler version -- and its fees are the lowest too. The criterion scored reward-for-risk and used the drop only as a do-no-harm check, so it cannot count the one thing that clearly moved. That is a flaw in how the criterion was written, and the fix is to write better criteria next time, not to rewrite this verdict after seeing the answer. HOW SURE ARE WE: it passes everything else -- both luck tests, beating every fake run on each; every one of its rolling start dates is profitable, and its worst start still beats the benchmark's typical one; it made money in all three periods of history; and nudging its remaining numbers around barely moves it. HOW IT COMPARES TO THE BIG ONE: it and the five-average strategy do not beat each other. That one earns more with a deeper hole and higher fees; this one earns less with a much shallower hole and the lowest fees. Neither is simply better, and choosing between them is a judgement about how much drop you can sit through, not an arithmetic question. A COST WORTH KNOWING: this was the fourth new idea tested in one session, and each one raises the bar every strategy here has to clear to be believed. That price is paid by all of them, including ones tested weeks ago. WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN: replayed past prices, never traded, no unseen data. Earns a trial run at most, and that call is the owner's.

This is a separate strategy standing on its own evidence. Read them together: the parent's failure and this one's result are two halves of the same finding, which is that gating on volume costs more than it earns. HOW SURE ARE WE: it now passes BOTH luck tests, beating every fake run on each, with the fakes losing heavily in both. Its earlier 'could not answer' was a fault in the timing test itself, since fixed. Its remaining numbers are not on a knife edge either. WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN: replayed past prices, never traded, no unseen data. Earns a trial run and nothing more, and that call is the owner's.

dist_sma_20 <= X is close/sma_20 <= 1 + X/100, i.e. "Price <= (1 + X/100) x Price MA 20". The threshold the recipe shows is already converted from idxbt's signed percentage (e.g. 10) to Stockbit's multiplier (1.1) -- typing idxbt's raw 10 into Stockbit would pass almost the whole market. NOT an exact equivalence, and this was measured rather than assumed: `python3 -c "import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_parquet('data/panel/ features_1d.parquet', columns=['close','sma_20','dist_sma_20']); a = df['dist_sma_20'] <= 10; b = df['close'] <= 1.10 * df['sma_20']; known = df['sma_20'].notna(); print((a[known] != b[known]).sum(), known.sum())"` currently prints `37 1257791` against the 2026-08-28 daily panel -- every disagreement sits at the exact tie close/sma_20 == 1.10, which is float64 rounding on a boundary, not a design gap. The other 302209 rows are NaN warm-up (no 20-bar SMA yet); `NaN <= 10` is False on both sides, so warm-up is excluded rather than admitted by either form. Re-run the command above against whichever panel is current rather than trusting this count. WHY verified IS false, and it is NOT because the mapping is doubted. Every PART of this rule is verified -- `Price` and `Price MA 20` are both verified Stockbit filters, and the `[field] [op] [multiplier] x [field]` shape is exercised by the verified `vol_ratio_50` mapping (`Volume >= 1.5 x Volume MA 50`). The COMPOSITION is not; nobody has opened Stockbit and typed `Price <= 1.1 x Price MA 20`. That is a deduction, and this file's own history is a list of deductions about screener fields that turned out wrong -- the retracted "atr" absence, and the Stoch RSI that exists and answers a different question. The term stays expressible and UNVERIFIED, which is what `Recipe.unverified` reports. ONE logged-in check flips it to true. Downgraded from verified:true on review, 2026-09-02.

Then rank by vol_ratio_20 — highest first, keep 10. No screener does this step, and it is not counted above.

Only screen when ihsg_above_sma_200 == 1 — a property of the index, not of any row. Check it once on a ^JKSE chart.

5 What every word here means

Every word the table uses, in plain language — including what each one does not tell you, which is usually the part that matters.

Start here

Promising?
Our own checklist, run automatically. Not an opinion, and not "whichever number is biggest".

Not a candidate — a measuring tool, never traded.
Unproven — never tested against random luck, or a luck test was run and could not give an answer. Those are different from failing one, and neither is a mark against the strategy.
Not promising — it loses money, or it fails the luck test, or it is worse than our best strategy on both reward-for-risk and worst drop. A bigger gain bought with a bigger hole is not an improvement.
Promising — makes money, beats luck, and is not worse on both counts.

Even "Promising" only earns a trial run. Every figure on this page comes from replaying past prices, and no strategy here has been traded with real money.
Seen as: Promising · Not promising · Unproven
Luck tests
Two tests of whether a result could have come from luck. Each one re-runs the strategy many times with one ingredient deliberately broken, keeping everything else the same — same exits, same fees, same Indonesian market rules — then asks where the real result lands among the fakes.

If the real run is not clearly better than the random ones, the broken ingredient was not doing any work. A strategy is starred only when it passes both. Passing one is common; passing both is not.

The documents call these null models.
Seen as: nulls S✓ T✓
Stock-picking test S
Keeps the days the strategy bought exactly as they were, and swaps in random stocks on those same days.

It asks: is the stock picking better than pulling names out of a hat? If random names on the same days earn about the same, the picking rule is decoration and the timing is doing all the work.
Seen as: S✓ passed · S✗ failed · S– never run
Timing test T
Swaps the days for random ones — and the stocks too, and ignores the market filter entirely.

It asks: is buying on these particular days better than buying on random days? This is the harder one, and the one most strategies fail. Failing it usually means the strategy was riding the market rather than timing it.

Sometimes this test cannot answer, and then it says so. The way it is built, the fake runs are handed as many candidate stocks per day as the real rule found that day. A picky rule hands them few and a loose rule hands them many — and the fakes then sort that bigger pile and keep the best of it, so they score higher for a reason that has nothing to do with the strategy. Comparing a loose rule against fakes that were quietly made stronger is not a fair test, so the answer is recorded as could not answer rather than as a loss. The stock-picking test above is unaffected.
Seen as: T✓ passed · T✗ failed · T? could not answer · T– never run
p-value
How often a random run matched or beat the real one. p≈.03 means about 3 in 100 of the fakes did as well — lower is stronger.

It has a floor set by how many times the test ran. With 12 runs the smallest possible answer is .077, however good the strategy is — the floor is 1/(N+1) for N runs. A weak-looking p from a short test is evidence of a short test, not of a weak strategy.
Forward test
Re-running the strategy on a stretch of time that was deliberately held back, to see whether it still works on prices it was never built against.

clean — the held-back period really was unseen.
contaminated — it was not. The strategy was built after its author had already looked at that period, so this is a consistency check and tells you nothing about the future. Recorded rather than hidden, because a contaminated test that looks clean is worse than no test.
not_run — it has not been done.
Seen as: fwd clean · fwd contaminated · fwd not_run

Reading the table

★ (star)
This one passed both luck tests. It is the strongest thing this project says about any strategy, and it still means one market, one stretch of history, and money that was never actually risked.
Screen
The list of filters you type into your screener. It is not one per strategy — several rows here share a single screen, because they differ in how they are traded or measured rather than in what they look for.

Rows with the same name here are one thing to set up in the morning. Each strategy's own section names the rows it shares with.
Seen as: Uptrend + Volume Surge
How to buy
The order you place once the screen has given you a name.

Market @ next open — buy at the next morning's opening price, whatever it is.
Limit @ prev close −2 ticks — leave an order slightly below last night's close and only buy if the price dips to it. It fills about 59% of the time on a trend strategy, because the names that take off never dip.

This choice is worth 86 percentage points of gain on our best strategy, which is why it gets a column instead of a footnote.
Seen as: Market @ next open
Chart
Which chart the strategy reads. 1d is daily bars, 1wk weekly. It matters more than it looks: a "50-period average" is 50 days on one and 50 weeks — nearly a year — on the other.

The documents call this the timeframe.
Seen as: 1d · 1wk
Total gain %
How much the account grew across the whole test, start to finish. Not per year — 180% over six years and 180% over one year look identical in this column. Fees are already taken out.
Worst drop %
The deepest fall from a high point to the low that followed it. Always negative: −35 means that at the worst moment the account was down 35% from its best.

This is the number that decides whether you could actually have held on. A gain you cannot sit through is not a gain you would have collected.

The documents call this maximum drawdown, or max DD.
Profit ÷ loss
Everything won divided by everything lost. Above 1.00 makes money; 2.00 means it won twice as much as it lost in total.

It says nothing about the shape — a 2.00 built from one huge winner and a hundred small losses is a completely different thing from a 2.00 built from steady small wins, and this column cannot tell them apart.

The documents call this the profit factor.
Trades
How many positions were opened and closed. A small number makes every other figure on the row unreliable: twenty trades cannot tell a strategy apart from luck, whatever its gain says.
Fees %
Everything paid to trade — commission, exchange fees, and the 0.1% Indonesian sell tax — added up across the whole run and measured against the account's average size over that run.

Average, not starting, size is deliberate. Charging every fee against the opening balance pretends the account never grew, when the fees grew because it did: a bigger account buys bigger positions and each trade costs more. Measured the old way, one strategy read 98% instead of 19% — same strategy, same fees.

A high number beside a high gain means the raw edge had to be big to survive its own trading.
Last run
When this strategy's test was last actually run. These are files on a disk; this is how old they are.
no run recorded
This one has never been tested, or its results were deleted. The row is left blank rather than showing zero — an unknown is never displayed as a result.

Warnings on a row

measuring tool
Not a strategy you would trade. It exists to measure another row — either by running the same rules a second way to prove both pick the same trades, or by switching one ingredient off to see what that ingredient was worth.

Left unlabelled, these sit in a table sorted by gain looking exactly like something you could buy. One of them currently shows the highest gain on the page.

The documents call these controls and ablations.
Seen as: instrument
alt entry
The same strategy as the row above it, bought a different way. Not a separate strategy, and it does not get counted as one.

It is shown only where buying that way still made money. On most strategies tried it did not.
Seen as: alt entry
STALE
This row's saved results are older than the price data they would run on. The figures describe an earlier version of the data and have to be re-run before anyone quotes them.
FILL NOT OBTAINABLE
This row's buy happens on the same bar as the signal, at a price that had not been published yet when the decision was made. Nobody could have earned its result. Flagged in the table rather than only in its own section, because the table sorts by gain and an impossible row otherwise lands among the winners.

Screening

TV and Stockbit columns
How many of the strategy's buying conditions each screener can actually set up, out of the total. 4 / 8 means four of its eight rules fit there and four do not.

These two columns are an EITHER, not a both. The house rule is that one screener must express the whole rule — either one is enough, and it does not have to be the same one for every strategy. So 3 / 5 on TV beside 5 / 5 on Stockbit is a strategy that fully passes: it is run on Stockbit. The low number is not a shortfall and it does not make the strategy "60% screenable".

What the low number does decide is where the screen is run. Running it on the screener that falls short would hand you a different rule's list, which is why the daily job names its platform.

A partial screen gives you a longer list: it can hand you extra names but never hides a real one. That is what makes it safe as a watchlist builder — and why it is not the strategy.
Seen as: 4 / 8 · 0 / 6
Ranking
A screen hands back a set of names; a strategy holds only its best few, chosen by sorting them on one column. No screener does this step, so it is left out of the fractions above.

When a strategy's buying rule is a loose floor, this sorting is the selection — so a high screener fraction on such a strategy flatters it.

The documents call this rank_by.
Market check
A condition on the index rather than on any one stock — for example "only buy while the IHSG is above its own 200-day average". It decides whether you open anything at all today, so you check it once on an IHSG chart instead of putting it in the screener.

The chart

Money over time
What the account would have been worth on each date.
Every line starts at 100
Each line is scaled to begin at 100, so strategies that started at different times and sizes can be compared by shape. A line reaching 250 has grown 150%. The index line is cut to the same window and scaled the same way, so it answers "would you have done better just buying the index".
log y / linear y
The vertical scale. On log, equal distances up the page are equal percentage moves, which is what makes a dozen lines spanning 100 to 1600 readable together. On linear they are equal rupiah moves, so the biggest line flattens everything else.

Appearance

Colour
Width
